title: Linked List Cycle
description: Brute force to optimized: tracking every visited node in a set versus Floyd's slow/fast pointer technique using O(1) space.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Given the head of a linked list, determine if the linked list has a CYCLE in it: some node's next pointer, followed repeatedly, eventually leads back to a node already visited earlier in the list.

blocks.caption: A slow pointer and a fast pointer moving at different speeds must eventually meet if a cycle exists

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given the head of a linked list, determine whether following its "next" pointers repeatedly ever leads back to an already-visited node, forming a cycle.

blocks.title: Analogy: Two Runners on a Racetrack of Unknown Shape
blocks.text: Like two runners on a track of unknown shape (it might be a straight dead-end path, or it might loop back on itself somewhere): one runner (slow) jogs at normal speed, the other (fast) sprints at double speed. If the track is a straight dead end, the fast runner simply reaches the end first and stops. But if the track loops back on itself anywhere, the fast runner, being faster, is guaranteed to eventually "lap" the slow runner and catch up to them from behind, since it gains ground on every single step while both are stuck circling the same loop.

blocks.caption: Inside a cycle, the fast pointer closes the gap to the slow pointer by exactly 1 node per step

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: values [3,2,0,-4], with the tail (-4) connecting back to index 1 (value 2)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Following next pointers from the head eventually revisits node value 2, then 0, then -4, then 2 again, forever","A cycle exists, starting at value 2","The tail node's next pointer points back into the list instead of to null"],["Answer","true","The list contains a cycle"]]}

blocks.text: Example: values [1], with no cycle (tail points to null)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Following the single node's next pointer immediately reaches null","No cycle exists","The list terminates normally"],["Answer","false","The list has no cycle"]]}

blocks.text: 5. How Should We Think?
Before storing every visited node in a set to check for a repeat, notice that two pointers moving at different speeds will behave very differently depending on whether a cycle exists.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If the list has NO cycle, the fast pointer (moving 2 nodes per step) will simply reach the end (null) before the slow pointer does, terminating the search cleanly.

Observation 2: If the list DOES have a cycle, once both pointers enter the cycle, the fast pointer gains exactly 1 extra node of relative distance on the slow pointer every single step (since fast moves 2 while slow moves 1, a net gain of 1 per step).

Observation 3: Since the cycle has some fixed, finite length, and the fast pointer's lead over the slow pointer (measured within the cycle) only ever increases by 1 each step (modulo the cycle's length), that gap must eventually become exactly 0 again, meaning the two pointers land on the exact same node.

Observation 4: So checking whether the slow and fast pointers ever point to the SAME node, at any step, correctly and definitively answers whether a cycle exists, using only 2 extra pointer variables.

Recognizing that a faster-moving pointer must eventually "lap" a slower one if and only if they're both confined to the same loop is the core insight that makes this two-pointer technique work, and is a broadly reusable idea whenever cycle detection is needed with O(1) space.
This is Floyd's cycle detection algorithm (the "tortoise and hare" technique): two pointers moving at different fixed speeds are guaranteed to meet if and only if a cycle exists.
6. Brute Force Solution
Track every node visited in a set, and check whether the current node has already been seen before.
Step by step algorithm

items: Walk through the list one node at a time, starting from the head.
At each node, check whether it has already been recorded in a set of visited nodes; if so, a cycle exists. Otherwise, record it and continue to the next node.

codes.python:
def has_cycle(head):
    visited = set()                                                        # remember every node object seen so far
    node = head
    while node:
        if id(node) in visited:                                            # revisiting a node means a cycle exists
            return True
        visited.add(id(node))
        node = node.next
    return False


if __name__ == "__main__":
    class ListNode:
        def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
            self.val = val
            self.next = next
    n1 = ListNode(3); n2 = ListNode(2); n3 = ListNode(0); n4 = ListNode(-4)
    n1.next = n2; n2.next = n3; n3.next = n4; n4.next = n2
    print(has_cycle(n1))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A set tracks visited node references directly (not values), since two distinct nodes could coincidentally share the same value.
The check for "already visited" happens before adding the current node, correctly detecting the exact moment a repeat occurs.
The walk terminates naturally at null if no cycle exists, since node eventually becomes None/null.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every node is checked against the visited set directly, so a cycle (if one exists) is always correctly detected.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), visiting each node at most once before either reaching null or detecting a repeat.
Space: O(n), for storing every visited node in the set.
Limitation: storing every visited node in a set uses O(n) extra space, when a pair of pointers moving at different speeds can detect the same cycle using only O(1) extra space.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force stores every visited node. Instead, use two pointers: slow, advancing 1 node per step, and fast, advancing 2 nodes per step. If fast ever reaches null (or fast.next is null), no cycle exists. If slow and fast ever point to the exact same node, a cycle exists, since this can only happen if both pointers are confined to looping around the same cycle.

Initialize both slow and fast to head. Repeatedly advance slow by 1 node and fast by 2 nodes, as long as fast and fast.next are both non-null. If at any point slow equals fast, return true immediately. If the loop exits because fast (or fast.next) became null, return false.
9. Optimized Solution
Advance a slow pointer by 1 and a fast pointer by 2 each step, checking whether they ever meet.
Dry run for values [3,2,0,-4], with -4's next pointing back to 2

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: slow and fast meet at the node valued -4 on step 3, confirming a cycle exists.

codes.python:
def has_cycle(head):
    slow = head
    fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next                                                   # slow advances 1 node per step
        fast = fast.next.next                                              # fast advances 2 nodes per step
        if slow == fast:                                                   # they can only ever meet if a cycle exists
            return True
    return False


if __name__ == "__main__":
    class ListNode:
        def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
            self.val = val
            self.next = next
    n1 = ListNode(3); n2 = ListNode(2); n3 = ListNode(0); n4 = ListNode(-4)
    n1.next = n2; n2.next = n3; n3.next = n4; n4.next = n2
    print(has_cycle(n1))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), since if no cycle exists, fast reaches null within O(n) steps, and if a cycle exists, the pointers meet within O(n) steps.
Space: O(1) extra, using only the 2 pointer variables.
Why This Works

If there's no cycle, the fast pointer (moving twice as fast) simply reaches the end of the list first, and the loop terminates via the null check. If there IS a cycle, once both pointers have entered it, the fast pointer's lead over the slow pointer (measured as a position within the cycle) increases by exactly 1 every step; since the cycle has some fixed length, this growing lead must eventually wrap around to exactly 0 again (a multiple of the cycle's length), at which point the two pointers occupy the exact same node.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["fast (or fast.next) becomes null","The list has no cycle; return false"],["slow and fast point to the same node","A cycle exists; return true immediately"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: Both pointers start at head, so no special-casing is needed for very short lists.
The loop condition (fast != null && fast.next != null) safely allows fast to advance by 2 without ever dereferencing a null pointer.
The equality check (slow == fast) compares node REFERENCES (or pointers), not values, which is essential since two different nodes could coincidentally share the same value.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Floyd's cycle detection (slow/fast pointers) is a fundamental technique whenever a cycle needs to be detected in a linked structure using O(1) extra space, based on the guarantee that a faster pointer must eventually catch up to a slower one if both are confined to the same loop.
Common mistakes

items: Comparing node VALUES instead of node references/pointers, which would incorrectly report a cycle whenever two different nodes happen to share the same value.
Checking only fast != null in the loop condition, forgetting fast.next != null, which can cause a null pointer dereference when advancing fast by 2.
Initializing fast to head.next instead of head, which works but requires extra care to avoid an immediate false "same node" match at the very start.

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly explain WHY the fast pointer is guaranteed to catch up to the slow pointer inside a cycle (it gains exactly 1 node of relative distance per step), since this justification is what separates truly understanding Floyd's algorithm from merely reciting it.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Detect a cycle in a linked list using O(1) space" points directly to Floyd's slow/fast pointer technique, rather than tracking visited nodes in a set.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you find the STARTING node of the cycle, not just detect its existence? This is Linked List Cycle II: after the pointers meet, reset one pointer to head and advance both at the same speed (1 step each); they meet again exactly at the cycle's start.
How would you find the LENGTH of the cycle? Once the pointers meet, keep one pointer fixed and advance the other by 1 step at a time, counting steps until it returns to the same node.

Could this technique detect a cycle in a DIRECTED GRAPH more generally, not just a linked list? The specific "same speed ratio catches up" argument relies on a single deterministic "next" pointer per node (a functional graph); a general directed graph with multiple outgoing edges per node would need a different approach (e.g., DFS with recursion-stack tracking).

12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Floyd's cycle detection: two pointers moving at different speeds (1 step vs 2 steps per iteration)
Core Idea: Inside a cycle, the fast pointer gains exactly 1 node of relative distance on the slow pointer every step, guaranteeing they eventually meet
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: A faster-moving pointer must eventually "lap" a slower one if and only if both are confined to the same loop
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: slow moves 1, fast moves 2; if they ever meet, a cycle exists
